name: TPS60400DBVR
title: TPS6040x unregulated 60 mA charge-pump voltage inverter, SOT-23-5
summary: A switched-capacitor inverter with no inductor: from a positive supply of 1.6 V to 5.5 V it makes a negative rail close to -VI, with no regulation, at up to 60 mA. A flying capacitor, an output capacitor and an input bypass are the only parts needed, and a start-up clamp that would otherwise be an external Schottky diode is built in. Four versions differ in oscillator: the TPS60400 lets its frequency move between about 50 kHz and 250 kHz with load and runs from 1 µF capacitors; the TPS60401, TPS60402 and TPS60403 run fixed at 20, 50 and 250 kHz. TPS60400DBVR is the TPS60400 on a 3000-piece reel.
key_figures: 1.8 V to 5.25 V recommended; 1.6 V min at TC ≥ 0°C
12 Ω typ, 15 Ω max at 25°C, VI = 5 V
35 mVP-P typ, TPS60400, IO = 5 mA, C(fly) = 1 µF, CO = 2.2 µF

notes: The R suffix orders a 3000-piece reel and the T suffix a 250-piece reel (TPS60400DBVR, TPS60400DBVT).
Automotive versions qualified to AEC-Q100 exist as TPS60400-Q1, TPS60401-Q1, TPS60402-Q1 and TPS60403-Q1.

circuits.title: Typical application
circuits.description: The basic inverter. C1 is the flying capacitor across CFLY+ and CFLY-, C2 bypasses the input and C3 holds the output. Any supply from 1.6 V to 5.5 V gives an output from -1.6 V to -5.5 V, loadable to 60 mA.

circuits.title: Voltage inverter, 5 V to -5 V
circuits.description: The same inverter set up for a 5 V input: the output is close to -5 V and may be loaded to 60 mA. All three capacitors are 1 µF; ceramic parts give the most output current and the best results with the TPS60400 and TPS60403.

circuits.title: Inverter supplying an op-amp load
circuits.description: The inverter powering the negative rail of an amplifier whose positive rail is VI. Before the pump has started, current through the load would pull OUT above ground; the device's built-in clamp holds it, so no external Schottky diode is fitted. The limit the device starts into is given by the maximum start-up current curve.

parts.note: pin 1 is its +V supply, pin 2 its -V supply

circuits.title: Inverter with RC post filter
circuits.description: An RC low-pass after CO trims the ripple further. R1 and C4 set the corner, fc = 1 / (2π × RP × CP); with 50 Ω and 0.1 µF the 250 kHz ripple is passed at 0.125 of its amplitude.
notes: The worked ratio uses RP = 50 Ω and CP = 0.1 µF at 250 kHz.

circuits.title: Inverter with LC post filter
circuits.description: An LC low-pass after CO, L1 in series and C4 to ground, for lower ripple and noise on the output.

circuits.title: Rail splitter, VO = VI / 2
circuits.description: The inverter turned into a divider that makes a mid-rail. The device's GND pin becomes the output and its OUT pin goes to system ground; C3 runs from VI to the mid-rail and C4 from the mid-rail to ground. The flying capacitor swaps between C3 and C4, keeping their voltages equal, so the output sits at half of VI and can feed dual-supply parts such as op amps. VI to ground (IN to OUT at the device) must stay at or below 6.5 V.

circuits.title: Doubler and inverter, -VI and about 2 × VI
circuits.description: One device gives both -VI and a positive rail near twice VI. CI, the flying capacitor and CO make the inverter; C3 and C4 with diodes D1 and D2 make a doubler fed from the CFLY+ node, with C3 as its flying capacitor and C4 as its output capacitor. Both outputs share the pump, so a load on either pulls both toward ground. The two output currents together must stay within 60 mA, the positive output within 30 mA, and less than that when the negative output is also loaded. Input current is about -IO + 2 × IO(POS).

parts.note: flying capacitor C(fly), polarised, + toward CFLY+
output capacitor CO, polarised, + to ground

circuits.title: Two devices cascaded for -2 × VI
circuits.description: U1 inverts VI to -VI on C3. U2 has its IN on ground and its GND pin on that -VI rail, so it inverts again from there and its output sits near -2 × VI with no load. The first device's output resistance times the second device's quiescent current lowers that a little. More than two stages make the output resistance climb steeply.

parts.note: U1 output capacitor, polarised, + to ground
U2 output capacitor, polarised, + to ground

circuits.title: Two devices in parallel
circuits.description: Two inverters share the input, the output and a single output capacitor, each with its own flying capacitor, which lowers the output resistance. CO is scaled by the number of devices, 2.2 µF with two devices.

parts.note: shared output capacitor CO, polarised, + to ground

circuits.title: Shutdown control through a buffer
circuits.description: An inverting logic buffer powered from VI supplies IN, so the SDN input turns the converter on and off. The output resistance becomes about 15 Ω plus twice the buffer's output resistance; several buffers in parallel lower it.

circuits.title: GaAs bias supply, -2.7 V at 3 mA from 3.3 V
circuits.description: A regulated negative bias. The inverter turns 3.3 V into about -3.3 V on CO; with a 0.1 µF flying capacitor its output resistance is about 52 Ω. R3 drops the rest and a TLV431 shunt regulator, its cathode on ground and anode on the output, holds -2.7 V set by R1 and R2. R3 with C5 also filters the ripple, to about 0.01 of its amplitude at 125 kHz. R3 may be at most 148 Ω; 100 Ω is used.

parts.note: This supply is specified with the TPS60403.

notes: R1 and R2 come from a 5 µA divider current: R2 ≈ 1.24 V / 5 µA, R1 ≈ (2.7 V - 1.24 V) / 5 µA.

circuits.title: Step-down charge pump, VO = VI / 2
circuits.description: Swapping the roles of OUT and GND makes a step-down pump: OUT goes to ground and the GND pin becomes the output. In one phase the flying capacitor and CO charge in series from VI and, being equal, split it; in the other they are put in parallel, so the output settles at VI/2. VI to ground (IN to OUT at the device) must stay at or below 6.5 V.

circuits.title: Step-down charge pump for 6.5 V to 11 V input
circuits.description: The step-down connection with a 5.6 V Zener diode from VI (cathode) to the output (anode), for inputs from 6.5 V to 11 V.

where.RSWITCH: on-resistance of one internal MOSFET switch
where.ESR_CFLY: series resistance of the flying capacitor
where.ESR_CO: series resistance of the output capacitor

equations.note: The first term is the resistance of an ideal switched-capacitor stage.

equations.name: Losses in the output resistance
equations.expr: PCAPACITOR LOSSES + PCONVERSION LOSSES = IO² × RO

equations.name: Conversion loss
equations.expr: PCONV.LOSS = [½ × C(fly) × (VI² - VO²) + ½ × CO × (VRIPPLE² - 2 × VO × VRIPPLE)] × fosc
equations.note: This loss arises when charge moves between C(fly) and CO while their voltages differ.

equations.name: Efficiency
equations.expr: η ≅ IO / (IO + IQ) × (1 - IO × RO / VI)
equations.note: Quiescent current sets the efficiency at light load and the output resistance at heavy load.

equations.name: Power dissipation
equations.expr: PD = VI × II - VO × IO = VI(max) × (IO + I(SUPPLY)) - VO × IO

where.I(SUPPLY): supply current, 0.7 mA max at full load

equations.note: Highest at maximum input voltage and maximum output current. Worked case: 5 V × (60 mA + 0.7 mA) - 4.4 V × 60 mA = 40 mW.

equations.name: Junction temperature rise
equations.note: 221 °C/W × 40 mW = 8.8 °C, so with TJ no higher than 125 °C the ambient may reach 115 °C (125 °C - 10 °C).

equations.name: RC post-filter ripple ratio
equations.note: Applies to the ac ripple only. With RP = 50 Ω, CP = 0.1 µF and f = 250 kHz the ratio is 0.125.

equations.name: GaAs supply output voltage
equations.expr: VO = -(1 + R1 / R2) × Vref - R1 × I(ref)

where.RO: inverter output resistance, 52 Ω with C(fly) = 0.1 µF

operation.text: Four internal switches run in two phases. First S1 and S3 close and the flying capacitor charges to VI. Then S2 and S4 close instead, putting the capacitor's positive end on ground and its negative end on the output, which charges CO negative. Switch resistance and the load's drain on CO leave the output somewhat above -VI. Low-ESR capacitors, ceramic for instance, give the best results.

A start-up flip-flop producing DC_Startup, an oscillator block (OSC, OSC CHG input, 50 kHz) feeding a phase generator that drives switches Q1 to Q5, and measurement blocks for VI, VO and the ratio VI / VO; the VI / VO block's VCO_CONT output controls the oscillator.
The device does not regulate. Its output source resistance is about 15 Ω at room temperature with VI = 5 V; with light load VO is near -5 V and it rises toward ground as load grows.

Three things cost efficiency: the IC's own losses (switch drive, oscillator), which depend on input voltage, temperature and frequency; resistive loss in the MOSFET switches and capacitor ESR; and the loss when charge moves between C(fly) and CO at different voltages. The second and third together equal IO² × RO.

The TPS60400 lets its switching frequency follow the load, from about 50 kHz at no load to around 250 kHz at high load, which cuts operating current where the load varies widely and allows small capacitors. Its power-save mode improves efficiency at low output current.

Between power-up and the moment the pump is running, a load connected from VI to OUT charges CO positive. An external Schottky diode across the output usually stops OUT rising above ground; this device has that clamp built in, giving defined start-up and saving board space. A modern op amp behaves like a current sink in series with a diode, and the device is designed to start into such loads, up to 25 mA at 1.25 V and 60 mA at 5 V across the load with the current starting at 0.4 V.

The basic inverter needs C(fly) and CO plus an input bypass if wanted. Three 1 µF ceramic capacitors give the most output current and best results with the TPS60400 and TPS60403; for less current or more ripple other values work. CO is kept at 1 µF or more, and a flying capacitor under 1 µF lowers the maximum output power. Low ESR in C(fly) and CO keeps the output resistance down. Using 1 µF parts of one type throughout is possible.

Bypassing the input lowers the supply's ac impedance and the switching noise it sees. With the load from OUT to GND the supply current jumps between 2 × IO and zero, so a large bypass, for instance equal to C(fly), suits a supply of high ac impedance. With the load from IN to OUT the draw is a steady 2 × IO apart from brief spikes, and 0.1 µF is enough.
A larger C(fly) lowers the output resistance and a smaller one raises it, up to a point where switch resistance and capacitor ESR dominate and more capacitance makes little difference.

A larger CO lowers the ripple, and lower ESR lowers both ripple and output resistance. Light loads can use a smaller CO if more ripple is acceptable. Ceramic types give the lowest ripple, having the lowest ESR.
With RθJA of 221 °C/W, the worst case of 5 V in and 60 mA out dissipates about 40 mW and raises the junction by under 10 °C, so with TJ limited to 125 °C the part can run at ambients up to 115 °C.
An RC or LC filter after CO lowers the output ripple and noise further.
The supply has no special demands; it only has to be rated for the input voltage, the output voltage and the load current of the converter.
Every capacitor is placed as close to the IC as possible, which keeps the output ripple low. A single-layer layout groups CIN, CFLY and COUT round the device.
A complete converter in the 5-pin SOT-23 fits in about 50 mm² of board.

LCD bias, GaAs bias for RF power amplifiers, sensor supplies in portable instruments, bipolar amplifier supplies, medical instruments and battery equipment. Typical inputs are a 5 V or 3.3 V rail, two or three NiCd, NiMH or alkaline cells, or one Li-ion cell. An evaluation module, TPS60400EVM-178, is available.
